questions.prompt: A colleague shows a rule with a one-year Sharpe ratio of 2.5. Which fact matters most for judging it?
options: Which programming language ran the backtest
Whether the Sharpe ratio was annualised with 252 trading days
Whether the rule is long or short more often
How many variants were tried before this one was kept
questions.explanation: The best of 100 no-edge rules has a middle best score of 2.49. A 2.5 from 100 tries is what luck alone produces; from 1 try it would be strong.

questions.prompt: In the example, the best of 100 random rules scored 2.63 in year 1. What did it score in year 2, and why?
options: -0.90, because its year 1 score was luck that did not repeat
2.63 again, because a good rule keeps its score
About 5, because Sharpe ratios add up over years
0 exactly, because a random rule always scores 0
questions.explanation: Every rule was a coin flip with a true Sharpe ratio of 0. Year 1 picked the luckiest one, and in year 2 it scored -0.90.

questions.prompt: You try 20 moving-average lengths and 5 holding periods, every combination. How many tries is that?
options: 100, because each length is tried with each holding period
20, because only the lengths are parameters
questions.explanation: Each combination is a separate backtest: 20 × 5 = 100 tries. Every parameter you add multiplies the number of tries.
